claims.text: A hybrid machine-learning potential calibrated with limited ab initio calculations and combined with thermodynamic integration can accurately reproduce solid- and liquid-phase free energies near melting.
The proposed framework can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling effects.
The framework will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
The cost advantage will be especially significant for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The machine-learning potential should be trained on targeted ab initio data representing both solid and liquid states.
Machine-learning interatomic potentials can be used in molecular-dynamics or Monte Carlo simulations of multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Thermodynamic integration driven by the learned potential can compute phase free energies and entropy contributions without full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The method is expected to operate over approximately 0.8–1.5 times the melting temperature.
The method is expected to apply across elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloy systems.
The learned potential-energy surface inherently encodes local lattice distortions and chemical disparities.
Encoding local lattice distortions and chemical disparities enables accurate reproduction of free-energy landscapes across solid–liquid phase boundaries.
A relatively small, judiciously selected ab initio training set can yield interatomic forces with fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio evaluations.
Replacing ab initio force evaluations with machine-learning-potential evaluations enables faster ensemble sampling in both solid and liquid phases.
Thermodynamic integration with the machine-learning potential recovers free-energy differences that include vibrational and anharmonic contributions.
The resulting free energies and fusion properties will have accuracy comparable to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The method will reduce computational cost by approximately one order of magnitude relative to full ab initio workflows.
The method will provide faster throughput than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Performance may degrade for systems with extreme electronic complexity or at temperatures far outside the calibration range.
A deviation greater than 10% from explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD in phase free energies or derived observables would falsify the hypothesis.
